terms.comment: Latin speaks of laws, not of legislation. To propose a law is lēgem ferre (Traupman 180), to carry it lēgem perferre (Traupman 179), to vote it down antīquāre (Cic. Off. 2.73; Traupman 180); for the single law, see law.

terms.latin: lēgis lātor (lēgum lātor), lēgis lātōris m.
terms.gloss: a legislator, the proposer of a law
evidence: Cic. Cat. 4.10: lātor lēgis Semprōniae (Lewis & Short, s.v. lātor)
terms.comment: Classical authors write it as two words (Lewis & Short); Traupman prints lēgislātor, which Valerius Maximus and the jurists use.
Traupman’s word; anciently found once, in the Vulgate, for the giving of the Law to Israel (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Perniciōsē enim Philippus in tribūnātū cum lēgem agrāriam ferret, quam tamen antīquārī facile passus est
phrases.english: Philippus did harm when, as tribune, he proposed a land law, though he readily let it be voted down
